title: Wall-Clock Time Used as Duration or Ordering Authority
pattern: Wall-clock timestamps (`SystemTime::now()` or similar real-time clock APIs) are treated as reliable evidence of elapsed duration, local lease/lock validity, or causal ordering of distributed operations, despite clock adjustment and cross-node uncertainty.
why_bad: Time-of-day clocks are continuously adjusted by NTP and can drift, jump backward or forward, or stall during virtualization pauses and garbage-collection sweeps [23:287, 144, 261], so locally computed intervals can come out negative, zero, too short, or excessively large, producing infinite loops, premature timeouts, or crashes [144, 145, 262]. Unsynchronized clocks cannot by themselves establish causal order across nodes, and a pause after a lease-validity check can permit a stale write even when the local measurement used a monotonic clock, leading to silent data corruption [23:287].
detection: Local-duration case: `SystemTime::now()`, `SystemTime::elapsed()`, or wall-clock timestamp subtraction controls a timeout, deadline, lease/lock interval, rate-limit window, or loop exit condition. Distributed-order case: wall-clock comparisons alone determine transaction/write order or causal precedence across nodes. Distinguish these cases before selecting a repair.
fix: Use a monotonic clock such as `Instant` for local elapsed intervals, timeouts, rates, and locally measured expiry, as monotonic clocks never go backward and are unaffected by NTP corrections [144, 251]. For distributed ordering, use the logical-clock or database ordering mechanism matching the required semantics: Lamport timestamps give a causality-consistent total order, vector clocks represent causal relationships and concurrency, and database-provided MVCC tokens order only within the database's scope [23:287]. For lease-protected writes, also enforce stale-owner rejection at the protected resource, for example through correctly validated fencing tokens; replacing `SystemTime` alone is insufficient.
source: *Designing Data-Intensive Applications* (Kleppmann), Chapter 8: Unreliable Clocks [23:287]; Martin Kleppmann, *Designing Data-Intensive Applications*, Chapter 8 (Unreliable Clocks) / passages [144, 145, 262]; Brendan Gregg, *Systems Performance*, Clock Drift / passage [9, 261].
